content: A chemical compound is a substance composed of two or more different elements that are chemically bonded together in a fixed proportion by mass. The atoms within a molecule can be held together by various types of bonds, including covalent bonds, ionic bonds, or, in rare cases, no bonds at all. For instance, water (H₂O) is held together by polar covalent bonds, while sodium chloride (NaCl) is an example of an ionic compound. There are exceptions to the general definition of a chemical compound. Certain crystalline compounds may be classified as chemical compounds even though their composition can vary due to the presence or absence of elements trapped within the crystal structure. Additionally, some compounds that are chemically identical may contain varying amounts of heavy or light isotopes of their constituent elements, causing slight variations in the mass ratio of the elements. As a result, a compound may not always be completely homogeneous. Not all molecules qualify as compounds. For example, a diatomic molecule of hydrogen (H₂) is homonuclear, meaning it consists of atoms of only one element, and therefore it is not considered a compound. Chemical compounds differ significantly from mixtures in terms of their physical and chemical properties. A compound's properties are distinct from those of its constituent elements, whereas a mixture's properties are generally similar to or related to those of its components. Furthermore, the constituents of a mixture can typically be separated by simple mechanical means, such as filtration, while the components of a compound are often much more difficult to separate. The formation of a compound involves a chemical change through a chemical reaction, whereas mixtures can be created through mechanical processes alone. Chemists use formulas to describe compounds in various formats. For molecular compounds, the formula represents the molecular unit, such as NaCl for salt. The order of elements in molecular and empirical formulas typically follows a convention: carbon (C) first, then hydrogen (H), followed by the remaining elements in alphabetical order. For example, trifluoroacetic acid is represented as C₂HF₃O₂. Structural information can also be conveyed through more descriptive formulas, such as CF₃CO₂H for trifluoroacetic acid. In contrast, formulas for inorganic compounds often do not provide structural details, as seen with H₂SO₄, which lacks H-S bonds. A more descriptive representation of this molecule would be O₂S(OH)₂. Elements form compounds to achieve greater stability. Stability is attained when an atom's outermost energy level is filled with the maximum number of electrons, typically two or eight valence electrons. This explains why noble gases rarely react; they already possess a full complement of eight valence electrons (with helium being an exception, requiring only two valence electrons for stability). Compounds can exist in various phases, including solid, liquid, gas, and, in some cases, plasma. All compounds can exist as solids at sufficiently low temperatures. Molecular compounds may also exist as liquids or gases under appropriate conditions. When heat is applied, all compounds decompose. The temperature at which decomposition occurs is referred to as the decomposition temperature. This temperature is not fixed and depends on the rate of heating. At sufficiently high temperatures, all compounds, either during or after decomposition, break down into smaller compounds or individual atoms. Every chemical compound described in the scientific literature is assigned a unique numerical identifier known as its CAS (Chemical Abstracts Service) number.
